title: The Calendar Blocking Method That Finally Made Me Feel in Control
script: The average knowledge worker checks their email 74 times a day and switches tasks 566 times. That's not working hard — that's working chaos. Calendar blocking is the opposite: you pre-decide what you'll work on and when, before the world fills your schedule for you. Start with your non-negotiables — exercise, sleep, deep work. Block those first. Then fill around them. A 90-minute deep work block is more valuable than 6 hours of scattered attention. Treat your calendar like your most valuable asset. Because it is.
prompt_for_hailuo: Messy digital calendar: dozens of tiny scattered event blocks, chaos [Screen close-up]. Hand drags and organizes blocks into clear color-coded sections [Montage of calendar being cleaned]. Calendar transforms: clear deep work blocks, meeting blocks, break blocks, all color-coded [Screen wide shot]. Person at desk during a blocked deep work session, fully focused, coffee untouched [Medium shot]. Clock shows 90 minutes passing, person completes major task [Montage of task completion]. Calm organized calendar, person's satisfied expression [Split screen: before chaos vs after control]. Minimalist home office, clean desk, natural morning light, portrait 9:16.
thumbnail_idea: Messy scattered calendar blocks vs clean organized color-coded blocks — 'FEEL IN CONTROL' text overlay
visual_scene: A clean home office desk with a laptop open to Google Calendar. The screen shows a chaotic, overwhelming calendar — dozens of tiny, disorganized event blocks scattered throughout the day in no discernible pattern. A hand reaches in and begins dragging and organizing: deep work sessions get deep blue blocks, meetings get orange, breaks get green, exercise gets purple. The calendar transforms into a beautiful, color-coded, intentionally structured day. The person sits at their desk during a 90-minute deep work block, completely focused, untouched coffee beside them. A clock animates showing 90 minutes passing quickly. The person completes a major task — a thick document checked off, code shipped, presentation done. Split-screen comparison: chaotic scattered calendar on the left, clean organized calendar on the right. Morning light fills the minimal home office. Portrait 9:16.
